children: Euronext wheat edged down from a one-week high on Thursday, curbed by weakness in Chicago grains and lingering hopes of military de-escalation in the Black Sea export zone.
on Euronext settled 0.4% down at €243.50 ($279.42) a metric ton after the day session.
The contract earlier rose to a one-week peak of €246, extending a rebound from Monday's September low of €238, before tracking Chicago futures
Chicago wheat, a global benchmark, eased as a slide in crude oil, strength in the dollar and renewed talk of diplomatic efforts for a Black Sea truce weighed on prices.

Traders said an AFP report, which cited a Turkish proposal sent to Russia and Ukraine for a truce on strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea, put attention back on potential de-escalation prospects.

However, traders were sceptical given that Turkey has already flagged such proposals and with a deal to halt strikes on energy infrastructure announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday showing little effect.

“Headlines today were again about diplomatic efforts to get some form of Black Sea safe shipping agreement, with Turkey said to be involved,” one German trader said. “But heavy attacks continue by both Russia and Ukraine and there is no concrete evidence of any deal, so price falls are moderate.”
Signs of continued Russian exports through the Baltic and Caspian seas were also tempering concerns about disruption to Black Sea trade.

Russian 12.5% protein wheat for nearby Baltic Sea shipment was offered around $269-$271 a ton FOB and 11.5% around $263-$265 a ton FOB in significant volumes, according to traders who said this was about $15-$16 a ton cheaper than Romanian and German wheat, and around $20 cheaper than French wheat.
Large long positions built up by investment funds in wheat and other crops also made prices prone to pullbacks.

"Speculators have been rushing into these markets, they hold record positions in key crops," Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, told reporters in Paris. "If we see any (supply) improvements, we could see a (price) correction."
The International Grains Council on Thursday raised its 2026/27 world wheat crop outlook, while noting that global wheat flows were unusually slow due to severe disruptions to Black Sea exports.
